title: Feudalism and manorialism in medieval Europe
summary: Feudalism is the name historians give to the bonds of lordship and land that ordered western European society between the eighth and fifteenth centuries. A lord granted a vassal a fief, usually land, in return for an oath of homage and service, often military; the Carolingian kings fostered the system. Its smallest unit was the manor, where the lord kept a demesne worked by serfs bound to the land by heredity. Historians still debate its roots, and it waned as monarchs built centralised states.

uncertainty.note: Emerged in the post-Roman and Carolingian era during the eighth and ninth centuries, persisting as the dominant agrarian and aristocratic framework until early modern centralized states and commercial markets displaced them.

as_recorded.value: used variously to describe legal, political, military, social, and economic features of western European society between the eighth and the fifteenth centuries.
